title: The quest for immortality has become serious business

vocab.articleQuote: a growing number of influencers peddle elixirs
vocab.meaning: To peddle something is to sell it, especially by going around promoting it, and the word often hints that the goods are cheap, dubious, or oversold. A peddler used to carry wares from door to door. In the article, influencers who peddle “elixirs” are pushing supplements and potions whose benefits are not proven.
examples: Online scammers peddle fake cures to worried people.
She refused to peddle rumours about her classmates.

vocab.articleQuote: One of the loudest evangelists is Bryan Johnson
vocab.meaning: An evangelist is someone who spreads a belief with burning enthusiasm, hoping to convert others. The word began in religion, for those who preached the Gospel, but now describes anyone who eagerly champions a cause, product, or idea. Here, Bryan Johnson is a longevity evangelist because he loudly urges people to adopt his anti-ageing routine.
examples: My uncle is a cycling evangelist who thinks everyone should ditch their car.
Early evangelists for the new app convinced their whole school to join.

vocab.articleQuote: scientifically proven ways to add healthy years—a far more arduous process
vocab.meaning: Arduous means demanding a lot of effort, endurance, and time, like climbing a steep mountain. It is stronger than “hard”: an arduous task wears you out and cannot be rushed. Proving that a drug really slows ageing takes years of trials, which is why the article calls the process arduous compared with simply selling supplements.
examples: The explorers made an arduous trek across the frozen plateau.
Writing a book is an arduous job that takes patience.

concepts.name: Biological age and ageing clocks
concepts.articleQuote: which estimate how old a body really is (as opposed to how many birthdays it has had)
concepts.meaning:
Biology. Your **chronological age** is simply the number of birthdays you have had. Your **biological age** is how worn-out your body is, and two people born on the same day can differ by years: one may have the arteries and energy of someone much younger, the other of someone older. Doctors cannot read biological age off a birthday, so scientists build **ageing clocks**: tests that measure chemical marks on DNA, or the mix of proteins in the blood, and compare them with patterns found in many people of known age. A body whose marks look like those of an average 50-year-old is said to be biologically 50, whatever its birth certificate says.

Why it matters here: testing whether a drug slows ageing by waiting to see who lives longest could take decades. A clock offers a quick stand-in. Novo's data put the heart's biological age up to four years younger in patients on its drug than in those on a **placebo** (a dummy treatment used for comparison).

The catch: a clock is a **proxy**, a measurement standing in for the thing we really care about, living longer and healthier. A proxy can move without the real outcome following, and the studied patients were overweight or diabetic, so it is unknown whether healthy people would see the same change.

concepts.name: Why ageing isn't a “disease” for drug approval
concepts.articleQuote: does not treat ageing as a disease, so there is no route to approving a medicine that slows it
concepts.meaning:
Regulation. Before a medicine can be sold in America, the **FDA** (Food and Drug Administration) must approve it, and approval is granted for a specific **indication**: a named medical condition the drug is shown, in trials, to treat safely. A drug is not simply “approved”; it is approved *for something*, such as diabetes. Ageing is not on the FDA's list of diseases, so a company cannot run a trial, show that its pill slows ageing, and get a licence.

That shapes the whole business. Companies pick a recognised condition linked to ageing, win approval for it, and then try to widen the drug's use. GLP-1s followed this path: first approved for diabetes, then obesity, and later shown to help hearts, kidneys and sleep apnoea, conditions that grow more common with age. Insilico's “dual-purpose” drug treats a lung-scarring disease while also being studied for ageing.

The unregulated side is the opposite: clinics and online sellers face no such test, so supplements and injections can be sold on hope and anecdotes. Regulators' rules create a gap between what is proven and what is for sale.

quiz.question: According to the article, what are the two very different industries chasing longevity?
options: Lightly regulated clinics and online sellers, and biotechs working with big drugmakers on medicines that might slow ageing
Insurance companies and hospitals
Gyms and restaurants
Governments and universities
quiz.explanation: The first is a colourful, lightly regulated group selling supplements, scans and treatments; the second is slower-moving biotechs developing real medicines in concert with drugmakers.

quiz.question: Why does the article say the FDA's stance makes longevity drugs hard to develop?
options: It bans all anti-ageing research
It does not treat ageing as a disease, so drugs must win approval for a specific condition first
It only approves drugs made in America
It requires every drug to cost less than $1,000
quiz.explanation: With no route to approve a medicine that slows ageing itself, would-be longevity drugs must treat a specific condition, often linked to ageing, and then expand.

quiz.question: What are “ageing clocks”?
options: Wristwatches that count your birthdays
Tests that estimate how old a body really is from chemical marks on DNA or proteins in the blood
Machines that slow down time in a clinic
Government records of life expectancy
quiz.explanation: Ageing clocks estimate biological age, as opposed to how many birthdays someone has had.

quiz.question: Why does the article suggest GLP-1 results should be treated cautiously?
options: The drugs were never tested on humans
All the patients studied were overweight or diabetic, so it is unknown whether healthy, slim people would benefit the same way
Novo and Lilly refused to share any data
The drugs make the heart older
quiz.explanation: The ageing-clock results came only from overweight or diabetic patients, and Lilly calls its own results preliminary.

quiz.question: What does “peddle” suggest in “influencers peddle elixirs”?
options: Carefully test
Sell or push, often goods of doubtful value
Give away for free
Ban
quiz.explanation: To peddle is to sell by promoting, often with a hint that the goods are dubious or oversold.
